items.title: Butch Miles interviewed by Monk Rowe, via Zoom, October 9, 2020 [interview 2 of 2]
items.q: my first teacher was a gentleman back in Charleston, West Virginia by the name of Frank Thompson.

ctx.x: And who might they have been?

Well my first teacher was a gentleman back in Charleston, West Virginia by the name of Frank Thompson. I sing Frank’s praises everywhere I have ever been, because Frank didn’t teach me a whole lot of the technique. He wasn’t saying okay now here you’re going to be going into a double paradiddle, and here are the specific drums that you hit within the specific timeframe of this paradiddle in 4/4. However, if you change it to 3/4 here’s your problem. We never got into that. We never did that. I fumbled around on…
Oh come on, you can tell us.

items.title: Butch Miles interviewed by Monk Rowe and Michael Woods, Scottsdale, Arizona, March 4, 1995 [interview 1 of 2]
items.q: Frank took me under his wing. He was a fine jazz drummer and immediately turned me in that direction. So I say Frank probably had so much influence on getting me into jazz

ctx.x: Well there’s no disrespect to Mr. Nelson, I just couldn’t stand his playing (sorry about the towel, it’s still dripping, does this come on the microphone, that’s all right we’ll get it later). I started out on a drum set playing the most banal rock ‘n roll, this was in 1959, 1958. And there was really nothing going on in rock ‘n roll exciting or creative, not like a lot of the wonderful, wonderful bands you’ve got now and the great drummers you’ve got now. It was all pretty cut and dried and very boring. But I…
and that got me further and I should say deeper and deeper into that style era of the ‘30’s, and the ‘40’s and the ‘50’s.
